description: We are a mixed team of CS and MIS students looking to collaborate and innovate together.
summary:
BASELINE is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support app for astronauts on long missions, where a reply from Earth can take many minutes. Before launch, each astronaut’s pre-flight data becomes a personal baseline. In flight, the crew log simple vital signs. The app instantly shows OK, WATCH or ACT NOW by comparing each reading to public medical limits and to that astronaut’s own normal.

When a flag appears, BASELINE lists possible everyday causes, such as short sleep, stress, fever or early adaptation, each with a cited source. On a red reading with chest pain, it opens an on-board protocol one step per screen. It also builds one structured SBAR handoff packet that reaches the flight surgeon after a simulated communication delay.

It addresses the challenge by keeping medical decision support on board when Earth is far away. That matters because Moon and Mars crews will need to act before help can answer.
details:
What it does and how it works

  • Personal baselines: 14 days of pre-flight data per astronaut set their normal. Every new reading is scored against absolute limits and against that baseline, in standard deviations, always shown with the sample size.
  • Instant status: OK, WATCH or ACT NOW, shown by shape, word and colour together, with the reason and the source of the limit.
  • Context-aware alerts: a rules file checks for known confounders (short sleep, missed exercise, the first 14 days, stress, fever, space weather, cabin CO2). Matching factors are shown with sources. A benign factor can only soften a yellow flag; red flags, temperature and oxygen are never softened, and nothing is hidden.
  • Urgent symptom protocols: opens on-board first when the delay is long, logs every step with mission time, and flags steps that need medical review. The app gives no drug doses.
  • SBAR handoff packet: readings, baseline, steps taken and pre-answered follow-up questions in one message, so the surgeon doesn’t have to ask questions one at a time over the delay. Ground sees how old the data is.
  • Reports and trends: biweekly and monthly reports with trend direction and a low-confidence label when data is thin.



Benefits and intended impact
Fewer false alarms, faster action on real ones, and less waiting on Earth. The same design fits remote clinics, Antarctic stations and ships with poor connectivity.

Tools and technologies
C# with ASP.NET Core and Entity Framework Core (SQLite); SvelteKit, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Apache ECharts; YAML configuration files for limits, context rules and the protocol; automated tests with dotnet test. It runs locally in a browser on a laptop or tablet, with no internet needed. AI coding assistants helped during development; the app itself uses no AI to make decisions.

Creativity

  • A personal baseline instead of one-size-fits-all limits.
  • Alerts that explain themselves and cite their sources.
  • A handoff format designed around the communication delay itself.
  • A crew interface built for gloved, tired hands: large controls, minimal typing, never colour alone.



Factors we considered

  • Safety: decision support, not diagnosis, and medical review flags on sensitive steps.
  • Credibility: every threshold and message traces to a public source (NASA, MedlinePlus, AHA, Mayo Clinic, CDC,...), or is marked as a team starting value.
  • Privacy: all crew data is synthetic, because real astronaut data is restricted.
  • Accessibility and offline use.
  • Application to general healthcare in remote areas and hostile areas
